## Overview

Coach Getsee asked us what his pitchers' stuff looks like, specifically their **movement profiles** and their **release profiles**. In class we built a movement profile for Nathan Hale. This week you'll build a short report for one other pitcher.

Your pitcher: Jayson Ingles

The report has two figures:

1.  his **movement profile** (what we did in class)
2.  his **release geometry**: where the ball leaves his hand

and a short note telling coach what to look at.

A few things:

1.  Add `#| echo: false` to your code blocks. Coach should see charts and words, not code.


We're using the same colors for every pitcher, so that a slider is the same color in every report coach gets. Run this as is. If your pitcher throws a pitch type that isn't here, add it.

```{r}
#| echo: false

okabe_ito <- unname(palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")[2:8])

pitch_colors <- c(
  "Fastball" = okabe_ito[1],
  "FourSeamFastBall" = okabe_ito[1],
  "Sinker" = okabe_ito[4],

  "Curveball" = okabe_ito[7],

)
```

```{r}
ingles |>
```

# Part 2: The report

Everything in this part goes to coach.

## His movement profile

> Make a movement profile for your pitcher that coach can read without you in the room. Use what we did in class: labels instead of a legend, how many pitches are behind each label, the raw pitches in the background, and a title that tells coach what to see.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
ingles <- ingles |>
  filter(TaggedPitchType == "Fastball" | TaggedPitchType == "Slider")

centers <- ingles |>
  group_by(TaggedPitchType) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    RelSpeed = mean(RelSpeed, na.rm = TRUE),
    HorzBreak = mean(HorzBreak, na.rm = TRUE),
    InducedVertBreak = mean(InducedVertBreak, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

centers <- centers |> 
  mutate(label = str_c(TaggedPitchType, " (n = ", n, ")"))

focus_colors <- c(
  "Fastball" = okabe_ito[1],
  "Slider" = okabe_ito[3],
  "ChangeUp" = "gray60"
)

ingles |>
  ggplot(aes(x = HorzBreak, y = InducedVertBreak, color = TaggedPitchType,
             shape = TaggedPitchType)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = pitch_colors) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_label(data = centers, aes(label = label), color = "black") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Jayson Ingles's Fastball vs Slider Movement",
       subtitle = "Fastball has 16 more inches of induced vertical break",
       x = "Horizontal Break (inches)",
       y = "Induced Vertical Break (inches)") +
  expand_limits(x = 28) +
  annotate("segment", x = 20, xend = 21, y = 2.01, yend = 2.01) +
  annotate("text", x = 22, y = 10, label = "16in", hjust = 0)  +
  annotate("segment", x = 20, xend = 21, y = 17.5, yend = 17.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 21, xend = 21, y = 2.01, yend = 17.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

## His release geometry

`RelSide` and `RelHeight` are where the ball leaves his hand, in feet: side to side, and how high. (Check the glossary for where 0 is.) Coaches care about this because if one pitch comes out of a different spot than the others, a hitter can pick it up early.

> Make a figure that answers: **does every pitch come out of the same place?** The design is up to you. A few things to think about:
>
> - Both axes are in feet. What did Wilke say about that?
> - The differences here might be small. Is a foot the right unit for coach?
> - Does coach need every pitch, the average for each pitch type, or both?
> - Each pitch type has to be the same color it was in your movement profile.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
ingles <- ingles |>
  mutate(RelSide_in = RelSide*12) |>
  mutate(RelHeight_in = RelHeight*12)

centers_2 <- ingles |>
  group_by(TaggedPitchType) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    RelSide_in = mean(RelSide_in, na.rm = TRUE),
    RelHeight_in = mean(RelHeight_in, na.rm = TRUE)
    )

centers_2 <- centers_2 |> 
  mutate(label = str_c(TaggedPitchType, " (n = ", n, ")"))

ingles |>
  ggplot(aes(x = RelSide_in, y = RelHeight_in, color = TaggedPitchType,
           shape = TaggedPitchType)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = pitch_colors) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Jayson Ingles's Fastball vs Slider Release Positions",
       subtitle = "Fastball and Slider Release Points are Similar",
       x = "Horizontal (inches)",
       y = "Vertical (inches)") +
  expand_limits(x = 22)

```

## A note for coach

> In **150 words or fewer**, tell coach what to look at in each figure and what it means for this pitcher. Include one thing he should be careful about (for example, how many pitches something is based on, or which pitch type column you used). From the "Fastball vs. Slider Movement" figure, we can see that fastballs from Jayson Ingles have on average about 16 inches more induced vertical break than Ingles' sliders. Ingles' fastballs also have 15 inches more horizontal break than the sliders, on average. The fastballs tend to break about 10 inches in one direction, while the sliders break 5 inches on average in the other direction. Regarding the release point, Ingles' fastballs on average have a slightly higher vertical position than the sliders. The two pitch types seem to be very similar in release positions and somewhat variable. The tagged pitch type was used for this analysis.
